description: A group of year 10 students and their teacher, being introverted nerds.
summary:
For our project we built ENOM, a website with two interactive globes side by side. One globe shows the Moon or Mars and the other shows Earth. You can click anywhere on the Moon or Mars, and our app pulls real NASA terrain data for that spot. It uses LRO LOLA elevation data for the Moon and MOLA data for Mars. Then it compares that terrain with places on Earth and shows you the closest matches, and the Earth globe spins to the best one.

The challenge asked us to find places on Earth that are similar to possible landing sites and bases on the Moon and Mars. Our app makes that first research step faster and easier to see. Using AI, it compares things like elevation and roughness factors, and then displays the best possible matches.

This matters because sending astronauts and rovers to space is really expensive and risky. If scientists can find Earth places that act like the Moon or Mars, they can test equipment and train crews here first. We were also careful to show where the data is limited, because a match is only a lead to research further, not proof.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
ENOM is a website with two 3D globes side by side. One shows the Moon or Mars and the other shows Earth. When you click a spot on the Moon or Mars, our backend downloads real NASA elevation data for that area. For the Moon that's LRO LOLA data, and for Mars it's MOLA data. It works out terrain features like height range, slope and roughness, then compares them with a catalogue of Earth places such as hyper-arid deserts, polar deserts, volcanic areas and caves. The best Earth matches are ranked and the Earth globe flies to the top one.

We also built a scorecard page where you can change how much each feature matters. On top of that, there's an image search that compares 50 Earth photos with 50 Mars photos. For this we used a pre-trained computer vision model called DINOv2, made by Meta. It doesn't generate anything or make decisions. It just turns each image into a list of 384 numbers that describe its visual features, like texture, edges and shapes. Our own code then compares those numbers to find which Earth and Mars images look most alike.

What are the benefits?
Researchers can explore possible Earth analogues in seconds instead of searching through lots of separate datasets. Everything is visual and interactive, so it's easier for students and the public to understand too.

What is the intended impact?
Before going to the Moon or Mars, NASA tests rovers, habitats and astronauts in similar places on Earth. Our tool helps with the first step, which is finding those places. Testing on Earth first could make missions safer and cheaper.

What tools did we use?

  • Python with FastAPI for the backend
  • React, TypeScript and Vite for the website
  • PyTorch with DINOv2, a pre-trained computer vision model, to pull visual features out of images (we used it as is and didn't train it further)
  • NASA data: LRO LOLA (Moon), MGS MOLA (Mars), Diviner (Moon temperatures) and USGS geology maps for Mars
  • Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data for Earth
  • Git for teamwork, and pytest, Ruff and mypy for testing and checking our code
  • Normal laptops, because the code runs on a regular CPU and can also use a GPU if you have one

How is it creative?
Most analogue lists are fixed, but ours lets you click any point and find matches on the spot. Putting two globes next to each other makes the comparison feel real. We also mixed two kinds of comparison, terrain data and visual image matching, which we hadn't seen done together before. All the terrain scoring and ranking logic is our own.

What factors did we consider?

  • Honest science: a match is only a lead to research further, not proof. The app shows where data is missing or weak, for example where Mars has patchy laser coverage.
  • Fair comparisons: we only compare data at the same scale and in the same units, and we don't compare raw heights between planets because they're measured differently.
  • Data limits: the Moon works from 75°S to 75°N and Mars from 44°S to 44°N, and the app tells you when a click is outside that.
  • Being able to repeat our results: we recorded where every piece of data came from, and wrote tests so other people can check our work.
  • Being open about our tools: we explain exactly what DINOv2 does in our project so nobody thinks the matching is doing more than it really is.
  • Ease of use: clear labels, interactive controls, and features that aren't finished are marked as unavailable instead of being hidden.

Use of AI
We used an AI tool (Claude) to help us write this project summary and description. We then edited it ourselves to add our own thoughts, experiences and achievements, and to make sure everything accurately describes what we built.
